title: Diary of a Mad Black Woman
full_review:
In "Diary of a Mad Black Woman" (Lions Gate), Kimberly Elise plays a grievously wronged wife struggling to piece together her shattered life and start anew.

Directed by Darren Grant, this woman-overcoming-adversity saga mixes emotional drama with dollops of dark-edged comedy, resulting in a moving -- if at times melodramatic -- and fitfully humorous affirmation of faith, family and forgiveness, the tone of which alternates between raucously zany and spiritually soaring.

Based on Tyler Perry's stage play of the same name, the story centers on long-suffering Helen McCarter (Elise), a woman married to a successful and wealthy but abusive and unfaithful Atlanta lawyer, Charles (played to coldhearted perfection by Steve Harris).

On the outside, of course, the McCarters are the picture of upper-class bliss. Charles feigns affection for Helen at an award ceremony in his honor, blowing her a kiss from the podium. But as Helen observes in her first of many "diary" voice-overs, "Looks can be deceiving."

The charade comes to an abrupt end on the night of their 18th wedding anniversary, when Charles shows up at their palatial home with a gold digger (Lisa Marcos) -- with whom he has sired two children -- and demands a divorce, literally dragging Helen out the front door when she refuses.

However, to prove that he is not completely heartless, Charles hires a U-Haul truck to take Helen and her possessions -- which he conveniently packed beforehand -- wherever she wants to go. The truck's sympathetic, cornrowed driver, Orlando (Shemar Moore), tries to comfort the understandably distraught Helen, and though their first encounter ends badly their paths keep crossing, with pity blossoming into friendship and eventually love.

With nowhere to go and no career skills, Helen ends up on the doorstep of Madea, a plus-size, pistol-packing neighborhood grandmother figure, and her crotchety, pot-smoking brother, Joe, both played by playwright Perry, appropriately aged and padded a la Eddie Murphy in "Nutty Professor II: The Klumps."

Slowly Helen begins to move past the pain and get her life back on track, taking a waitressing job and enjoying strolls through romantic montage sequences with Orlando (many of which resemble cheesy music videos -- not surprising since that is the medium in which Grant cut his directorial teeth).

But not until a role-reversing twist of fate reunites Helen and Charles does she realize that the road to inner healing demands letting go of the vengeful anger and soul-withering bitterness that have kept a chance at happiness beyond her reach.

Rounding out the colorful ensemble are Cicely Tyson as Helen's churchgoing mother; Perry, yet again, as her loyal cousin, Brian; and Tiffany Evans as Brian's junkie wife and Helen's childhood best friend.

Though the movie deals specifically with experiences of an African-American family, its themes of recovery, revenge and redemption are universal.

Given Catholic teaching on marriage and divorce, some viewers may object to the film's resolution. Still, with its rousing gospel score, it is hard to find fault with the movie's overall celebration of faith as a source of strength in times of personal pain (a view which sustained a struggling Perry when he found himself homeless early in his writing career).

And while the film seems to suggest that Helen and Orlando do consummate their relationship, an earlier scene finds Helen confiding to her diary -- and the viewers -- that though they wanted to make love they already shared something far deeper than sex: intimacy.

Elise gives a strong performance, one that in many ways echoes her role in last year's "Woman Thou Art Loosed," which, coincidentally, was adapted for the screen by Perry from the book by Bishop T.D. Jakes, head of a nondenominational church. Both movies take faith seriously and deal with the healing power of forgiveness, reminding us that mercy is the source of true justice, one which frees both victim and offender.

The film contains some violence, including domestic abuse, mature thematic elements, an implied sexual encounter, brief drug content, and crude sexual language and humor. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
